title: A Boon Won in the Night
story:
The truce at nightfall was Krishna's doing.

All day, over the Parijata — the wish-giving tree of heaven, uprooted from Indra's own garden — the king of the gods had fought from the back of his elephant Airavata, and Garuda had met him with beak and claw until the great beast swayed, bleeding, in the sky. Now the sun had gone down behind the Parijatra mountain, the battle had begun again, and Krishna, looking across at the wounded elephant, raised his hand.

"Airavata is sorely wounded," he called to Indra, "and night grows apace. Let us refrain from fighting now. Do as you wish tomorrow morning."

The king of the gods saw the sense in it and agreed.

The mountain on which they camped had made itself small when Krishna came, sinking into the earth until it was no bigger than a stone for grinding sandal — a bow of reverence from a peak that knew whose weight it carried. Indra raised a shelter of stones for the night near the sacred Pushkara lake, and there Brahma came to him, and the sage Kashyapa with Aditi, and the hosts of heaven: the Sadhyas and the Vasus, the Ashwini twins, the Adityas and the Rudras. Krishna stayed on the far side of the mountain with his son Pradyumna and the warrior Satyaki, and behind them, resting on Garuda's back, stood the great Parijata itself, its blossoms pale in the failing light.

Before the night settled, Krishna turned to the mountain under him. It had bowed itself for his sake, and he would not let such reverence pass unmarked. "You shall be called Sanapada," he said, "and you shall be auspicious and holy as the Himalaya. Abound in gems; outvie Meru itself. I shall be glad to see you, always, full of precious stones."

Then, saluting the god whose emblem is the bull, Krishna thought of the Ganga — and at his thought the river that has its source in Vishnu's own feet came flowing up the mountain to him. He worshipped her, bathed in her water, and taking up that sacred water and leaves of the bilva tree, he offered them and invited Rudra, lord of all lords, to be present.

Shiva came. He appeared there with Uma at his side and his followers around him, manifest upon the surface of the Ganga's water and upon the bel leaves themselves. Krishna worshipped him with flowers of the Parijata — the very tree that had set heaven and earth at war — and then, in a voice that carried across the dark water, he eulogized the lord of lords.

"You are Rudra," he said, "for you bind beings in maya and release them, and you manifest through the sound that pervades the universe at birth; you are self-manifest. You are Pasupati, lord of all creatures, of those who hold to life and those who have renounced it. You are the performer of all acts; no master of the universe is your superior. You are the beginning, the giver of life, the cause of contentment of all the great masters, and so the learned call you the God of gods. Because all manifest creation is begotten of you, you are Bhava, the source from which all is born — self-created, creator of all creators. The defeated gods and asuras crowned you, and so you are Maheswara, the maker of the universe. I resign myself entirely to your protection. Crown me, who am devoted to your devotees and beloved of your beloved, with fame."

The night held still. When the hymn was done, the god of gods looked on Krishna and spoke.

"O best of gods, you shall obtain the things you desire. You shall carry away the Parijata tree. And you shall be invincible."

Then Shiva and Uma faded back into the night from which they had come, and Krishna was left on the moonlit bank with the water moving at his feet. The war over the tree had been fought with arrows and with claws; it would end, he knew now, with the tree going home with him.
reflection: Krishna spends the pause in the fighting not in readiness but in worship, saluting the god whose devotee he declares himself to be. The boon he wins is quietly telling: he asks that the Parijata be carried away and that he remain invincible — as though the night's devotion, not the day's arrows, were the real weapon in the quarrel.
next_story_tease: But Shiva had not finished speaking: before the night was over he would tell Krishna what lay hidden beneath the mountain.
hero_scene: By night on the Parijatra mountain, Krishna stands at the edge of the Ganga with water and bilva leaves in his offered hands, as Shiva and Uma appear radiant upon the dark water, the moonlit Parijata tree blooming on Garuda's back behind him.
